power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Purpose: This study compared inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and jaw across talkers with Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurotypical controls (CON)     to identify disease-related differences.

The study also explored if a talker's tongue body cycle duration, which serve as a proxy for a talker's habitual speech rate, or a talker's reliance on their jaw, as indicated by their jaw movement amplitude, could predict their inter-articulatory timing patterns.

Method: Using three-dimensional electromagnetic articulography, the movements of the posterior tongue and jaw were examined in 24 talkers with PD, 19 talkers with ALS, 18 talkers with HD, 18 talkers with MS, and 34 CON during a sentence repetition task ("Buy Kaia a kite").

The tongue movement during the segment [kai]     served as the reference signal (tongue body cycle) for which the phase angle of the jaw reaching the maximum opening position during [kai] was calculated.
Tongue body cycle durations were measured as the time between the tongue body movement onset to the tongue body movement offset.

The jaw opening amplitude was measured as the relative positional change from the jaw's maximum closing position associated with [k]  to the jaw's maximal opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai].
Results: A significant group effect was found for phase angles.

Pairwise comparisons showed that talkers with ALS had significantly larger phase angles than talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON, indicating a timing pattern where the tongue reached the target [a] earlier relative to the jaw.
No significant differences were found.
Speech production is a complex goal-directed motor behavior that requires a smooth interaction of multiple speech subsystems (i.e., respiration, phonation, resonance, and articulation).
At the articulatory level, motor execution is carefully timed across the tongue, upper and lower lips, and the jaw, to achieve the desired acoustic output [1] [2] [3].

text.text: These inter-articulatory timing patterns are thought to play a critical role in the production of intelligible speech [4, 5].
text.formatted: These inter-articulatory timing patterns are thought to play a critical role in the production of intelligible speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: They can also provide insights in the spatiotemporal programming and coordination strategies of the motor control system.
In this study, inter-articulatory timing is understood as a specific, quantifiable aspect of speech motor coordination that describes how distinct speech structures are spatiotemporally aligned.

While closely linked to coarticulation, the context-specific physiological overlapping of adjacent speech gestures executed by one articulator, inter-articulatory timing focuses precisely on the coordination between two or more articulators.

Inter-articulatory timing patterns can be quantified by relative phasing, expressed as the positional and spatiotemporal state of one articulator relative to another articulator at a specific landmark in terms of a phase angle [6] [7] [8] or temporal latencies, expressed as the absolute time difference between articulatory events (velocity peaks, positional targets) of two articulators [8, 9].

text.text: This work focuses on the former, quantifying the relative phasing of the jaw relative to the tongue via phase angles.
In previous studies on neurotypical talkers, phase angles have been used to examine spatiotemporal relations between two articulators.

In such analyses, the movement of one articulator (typically the jaw) served as the reference signal, to which lip or tongue tip movements were related during consonant-vowel-consonant sequences such as [bab] or [tat]  [10, 11].

text.text: The rationale for a target utterance with two stop consonants was that it provided robust discrete kinematic landmarks to define the movement cycles.
The calculation of phase angles is based on the concept that articulators are oscillators producing sinusoidal-like movement cycles along a phase plane [6].
text.formatted: The calculation of phase angles is based on the concept that articulators are oscillators producing sinusoidal-like movement cycles along a phase plane <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the relative timing between two articulators can be quantified as phase angles.
In this framework, a phase angle of 180 degrees signifies a synchronized timing pattern.

Phase angles less than 180 degrees indicate that the reference articulator lags behind the second articulator, while angles greater than 180 degrees suggest that the reference articulator leads the second articulator.
This approach provides a nuanced representation of the spatiotemporal relationship between articulators during speech production (Fig. 1).

In their seminal work, Tuller and Kelso [12] examined inter-articulatory timing patterns of the upper and lower lip movements relative to the jaw cycle and reported relatively stable phase angles that were not affected by changes in jaw cycle duration (which were typically used as a proxy for quantifying a change in speaking rate or lexical stress).

text.text: By contrast, the majority of studies conducted later on suggested that the timing patterns do change when talkers manipulate their lexical stress patterns or speech rate [7] [8] [9] 13, 14].
text.formatted: By contrast, the majority of studies conducted later on suggested that the timing patterns do change when talkers manipulate their lexical stress patterns or speech rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14]</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, speech demands that resulted in a shortening of the jaw cycle duration (e.g., fast speech, unstressed segments) also decreased the phase angle.

Along those lines, speech demands that facilitated longer jaw cycle durations (e.g., slow speech, stressed segments) were associated with an increase in the phase angle, given that movement cycle duration serves as an established proxy measure for speaking rate.
However, a great deal of variability was noted across talkers and across different articulator pairs [12, 15].
text.formatted: However, a great deal of variability was noted across talkers and across different articulator pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, while upper lip timing maintained a relatively stable phase angle range relative to the jaw, tongue tip phase angles exhibited much greater fluctuations [7, 13].
text.formatted: Specifically, while upper lip timing maintained a relatively stable phase angle range relative to the jaw, tongue tip phase angles exhibited much greater fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, tongue tip phasing remained sensitive to rate, consistently varying with jaw cycle duration despite a greater underlying variability.
Temporal latencies refer to the temporal lag between kinematic trajectory landmarks purely in the time domain, independent of the articulators' positions and velocities.
Previous studies investigated tongue tip -jaw and lower lip -jaw timing patterns during the production of disyllabic utterances in neurotypical talkers [9, 10, 11, 16, 17].

text.text: In these studies, temporal latencies were measured as the time elapsed from the onset of the jaw vowel cycle until the initiation of the upward movement (raising) of the tongue tip or lower lip toward the intervocalic consonant [9, 11].
text.formatted: In these studies, temporal latencies were measured as the time elapsed from the onset of the jaw vowel cycle until the initiation of the upward movement (raising) of the tongue tip or lower lip toward the intervocalic consonant <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: An important finding of these studies was that a shortening of the jaw opening-closing cycle due to speaking rate or lexical stress manipulations systematically reduced the movement onset latency of the second articulator as well.

These precise temporal regularities held true across different sets of articulators (tongue-jaw and lip-jaw synergies), which suggests that synergistic timing patterns of vocal tract constriction formations are precisely controlled regardless of where in the vocal tract the constriction occured [10, 16, 17].

text.text: Only a limited number of kinematic studies are currently available that have examined inter-articulatory timing patterns and the majority of them investigated neurotypical talkers.

However, it is commonly assumed that inter-articulatory timing patterns are disrupted in talkers with dysarthria, a neurogenic motor speech disorder that arises when one or more neural components of the speech motor system are affected by a neurological condition.
Rather than presenting as a uniform deficit, dysarthria encompasses distinct subtypes depending on the neural components that are affected.
In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), for example, upper and lower motoneurons of bulbar and spinal muscles degenerate, which results in a mixed flaccid-spastic dysarthria.
Hallmark symptoms are an abnormally slow speaking rate, imprecise consonants and distorted vowels, and a strained-strangled voice quality [18, 19].
text.formatted: Hallmark symptoms are an abnormally slow speaking rate, imprecise consonants and distorted vowels, and a strained-strangled voice quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: Multiple sclerosis, by contrast, commonly affects the corticobulbar tract and cerebellar motor control circuits, which can result in a mixed dysarthria with spastic and ataxic components.
Common perceptual speech characteristics of talkers with MS include a slow speaking rate, irregular articulatory breakdowns, consonant imprecision, and a breathy or harsh voice quality [18, 20].
text.formatted: Common perceptual speech characteristics of talkers with MS include a slow speaking rate, irregular articulatory breakdowns, consonant imprecision, and a breathy or harsh voice quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: In other diseases, such as Parkinson's disease (PD) and Huntington's disease (HD) basal ganglia control circuits are commonly affected.

PD typically results in hypokinetic dysarthria, which is associated with an accelerated speech rate, short rushes of speech, reduced vocal loudness or loudness decay, a breathy or harsh voice quality, and consonant imprecision [20].
text.formatted: PD typically results in hypokinetic dysarthria, which is associated with an accelerated speech rate, short rushes of speech, reduced vocal loudness or loudness decay, a breathy or harsh voice quality, and consonant imprecision <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, speech disturbances in Huntington's disease (HD) typically manifest as hyperkinetic dysarthria and are characterized by involuntary movement intrusions, a variable speech rate, consonant imprecision, and irregular articulatory breakdowns.
Only few kinematic research studies are currently available on inter-articulatory timing patterns in neurogenic populations, such as individuals with PD and ALS.
These studies have provided crucial insights into how two neuropathologies can differentially alter inter-articulatory timing patterns [21, 22].
text.formatted: These studies have provided crucial insights into how two neuropathologies can differentially alter inter-articulatory timing patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, Weismer et al. (2003) investigated labial and lingual timing patterns by means of temporal latencies.
text.formatted: Specifically, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Weismer et al. (2003)</ref> investigated labial and lingual timing patterns by means of temporal latencies.

text.text: They reported that overall timing patterns of the tongue and lips remained largely unaffected in PD; however, individuals with ALS exhibited a significantly wider range and greater disruption of lip and tongue timing patterns [22].
text.formatted: They reported that overall timing patterns of the tongue and lips remained largely unaffected in PD; however, individuals with ALS exhibited a significantly wider range and greater disruption of lip and tongue timing patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Extending these observations to a spatiotemporal metric, Rong and Heidrick (2021) found that relative phase relationships between the tongue and jaw served as robust markers of bulbar involvement, with relative phasing achieving high diagnostic accuracy in differentiating individuals with ALS from healthy controls [21].

text.text: Beyond neurodegenerative conditions, there is only one kinematic study currently available that examined inter-articulatory timing patterns in talkers with dysarthria resulting from traumatic brain injury.
That study found no significant group-level differences in inter-articulatory timing patterns between nine talkers with traumatic brain injuries and nine typical talkers [23].
text.formatted: That study found no significant group-level differences in inter-articulatory timing patterns between nine talkers with traumatic brain injuries and nine typical talkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, an inspection of individual performance patterns revealed disrupted inter-articulatory timing patterns in those talkers with traumatic brain injury who displayed the most severe dysarthria symptoms.
Given the small sample size, this study offers very limited insights into how inter-articulatory timing patterns vary more broadly across of talkers with dysarthria.

Given the limited kinematic literature on speech motor control in talkers with dysarthria, the current study sought to investigate inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and the jaw in talkers with dysarthria with different neurological conditions [i.e., PD, MS, ALS, HD].

The comparisons across these four disease types are particularly interesting and important because these diseases are associated with different neuropathologies (i.e., differential disruptions to the basal ganglia control circuits in PD versus HD; disruptions to the direct motor pathway in MS and ALS, but additional cerebellar control circuit disruptions in MS).
Thus, these four different neurological conditions may give rise to disease-specific deviancies in interarticulatory timing patterns.

It is especially important to investigate the interarticulatory timing patterns of the tongue body and jaw in these talkers because tongue and jaw motor performance deficits have been reported in talkers with PD, HD, MS, and ALS [24] [25] [26] [27] [28] [29] [30].
text.formatted: It is especially important to investigate the interarticulatory timing patterns of the tongue body and jaw in these talkers because tongue and jaw motor performance deficits have been reported in talkers with PD, HD, MS, and ALS <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: For example, talkers with ALS are thought to produce excessive jaw movements to compensate for impaired tongue muscles during speech production.
An overreliance on the jaw may result in more synchronized tongue and jaw movements in these talkers as indicated by phase angles close to 180 degrees.

By contrast, talkers with MS, PD, and HD may exhibit less synchronized tongue and jaw movements considering that lesions in cerebellar and basal ganglia motor control circuits have been associated with the disruptions of temporal patterns during speech production [26, 30].
text.formatted: By contrast, talkers with MS, PD, and HD may exhibit less synchronized tongue and jaw movements considering that lesions in cerebellar and basal ganglia motor control circuits have been associated with the disruptions of temporal patterns during speech production <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, these talkers may have phase angles that are below or above 180 degrees.
However, it is also possible that inter-articulatory timing patterns of talkers with MS and ALS differ from those of talkers with PD due to differences in their speaking rate.
Based on the known speech motor profiles of different dysarthria subtypes, distinct timing disruptions may exist.

That is, talkers with PD may exhibit inter-articulatory timing patterns that mimic the timing patterns of healthy controls when asked to speak at an accelerated rate (fast speech), while talkers with MS and ALS may exhibit timing patterns that mimic those of controls when asked to speak at a reduced rate (slow speech).
Finally, the speech rate of talkers with HD is commonly described as variable [24], which may disrupt inter-articulatory timing patterns of these talkers in unpredictable ways.
text.formatted: Finally, the speech rate of talkers with HD is commonly described as variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>, which may disrupt inter-articulatory timing patterns of these talkers in unpredictable ways.

text.text: In sum, the aims of the current study were: • Aim 1: To characterize speaking rate of talkers with dysarthria, we determined between-group differences in tongue body cycle durations across clinical groups and controls • Aim 2: To characterize the reliance on the jaw in talkers with dysarthria, we determined between-group differences in jaw amplitudes across clinical groups and controls • Aim 3: To characterize inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and jaw in talkers with dysarthria, we determined between-group differences in phase angles across clinical groups and controls • Aim 4: To determine if differences in speaking rate account for differences in inter-articulatory timing patterns in talkers with dysarthria, we evaluated the association between tongue body cycle durations and phase angles.

• Aim 5: To determine if differences in the reliance on the jaw account for differences in inter-articulatory timing profiles in talkers with dysarthria we evaluated the association between jaw amplitude and phase angle.

text.text: All talkers with dysarthria presented with a perceptible articulatory subsystem impairment as indicated by perceptible imprecise speech, phoneme prolongations, phoneme repetitions, and/or an abnormal speaking rate during at least one of the following speech tasks: SIT, paragraph reading, or picture description.
The presence of an articulatory subsystem impairment was determined based on consensus ratings of two speech language pathologists (SLPs, one being the second author).
In five cases, a third SLP was included to reach a consensus.
All participants with PD and six out of 18 participants with HD were on medication that aimed to reduced motor-related disease symptoms at the time of data collection.
Three participants with PD had been treated surgically with deep brain stimulation (DBS) and were recorded while the device was turned on.
Kinematic speech data were recorded with an electromagnetic articulograph (AG 501; Carstens Medizinelektronik GmbH).
Small sensors were attached to the articulators to track their movements during speech.
That is, one sensor was attached with a small amount of Stomahesive® putty to the gumline of the lower central incisors to track jaw movements.
Additional sensors were placed at midline on the vermillion border of the upper and lower lips using dental adhesive (Periacryl 90, GluStitch).
Two sensors were placed with dental adhesive on the tongue.
One tongue sensor was attached approximately 1 cm posterior to the tongue tip to track its movements.
The other tongue sensor was placed approximately 4 cm posterior to the tongue tip to assess tongue body movements.
Three additional sensors were placed on plastic goggles (head right, head center, head left) that the participants wore during data collection.
These sensors served as reference sensors for head correction [28].

text.text: Finally, three sensors were placed on a biteplate, which participants were asked to hold between their front teeth to record a short rest file.
After attaching all sensors, participants were engaged in conversations to provide them the opportunity to familiarize themselves with the presence of the sensors in the oral cavity.
Afterwards, the experimental protocol was started.
As part of a larger experimental protocol, participants were asked to produce the sentence "Buy Kaia a kite", which was displayed on a computer monitor in front of them.
All participants were asked to repeat the sentence ten times at their typical speaking rate.
"Kaia" was produced as /'kai. ə/.
If a participant did not produce the word "Kaia" correctly, the examiner modeled the correct pronunciation and ask the participant to repeat the task.
The raw data were converted into positional data using the CalcPos software (Carstens Medizintechnik GmbH).
Then all positional data were head-corrected, down-sampled to 250 Hz, and transposed into a head-based coordinate system using the NormPos software (Carstens Medizintechnik GmbH).
Data were filtered with a low-pass filter at 15 Hz and displayed and further processed in SMASH, a MATLAB-based software program [34].

text.text: The data analysis focused on the first, stressed syllable of the word "Kaia", consisting of a stop consonant and a diphthong (/'kai.
For the purpose of this study, only the tongue body and jaw movement in the vertical dimension (i.e., y-dimension) were considered.

Within the movement sequence of the tongue body during the syllable [kai], the onset of the jaw raising movement during the diphthong [ai] can be determined as an angle on the tongue body's phase plane.

The segment [kai] was of particular interest in this study because, although the tongue body and jaw are anatomically coupled, the tongue and the jaw can independently reach the maximum vocal tract opening at the onset of the diphthong different times and, consequently, initiate the movements towards the maximum vocal tract closing at the offset of the diphthong at different times.

Furthermore, the inter-articulatory timing patterns of the jaw and tongue body were also of interest because the velar place of articulation has been shown to be affected at the early stages of articulatory performance decline in talkers with neurodegenerative diseases [35].
text.formatted: Furthermore, the inter-articulatory timing patterns of the jaw and tongue body were also of interest because the velar place of articulation has been shown to be affected at the early stages of articulatory performance decline in talkers with neurodegenerative diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: We did not decouple the jaw from the tongue in the current study.

An estimation of independent tongue movement based on linear subtraction of the jaw movement would have resulted in an overestimation of the jaw contribution due to the jaw sensor's location being more anterior from the center of the jaw rotation than the posterior tongue sensor's location [36].
text.formatted: An estimation of independent tongue movement based on linear subtraction of the jaw movement would have resulted in an overestimation of the jaw contribution due to the jaw sensor's location being more anterior from the center of the jaw rotation than the posterior tongue sensor's location <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the phase angles reported here describe the relationship of the jaw relative to the tongue body+jaw composite movement rather than to an independently derived tongue body movement.

While individual differences in the intrinsic contribution of the jaw to tongue movement could not be fully captured without decoupling, pilot trajectory inspections confirmed consistent asynchrony between jaw and tongue positional minima.
Thus, the phase angles in this study represent only the relative phasing of the jaw in relation to the tongue body+jaw movement during the syllable [kai].
Contrary to most previous studies in which the jaw cycle was used as a reference, in the current study the reference for the phase angle calculation was the tongue body cycle.
For the selected target word, the jaw could not be used as a reference because its movement did not offer a reliable landmark for the cycle offset.
Instead, the vertical movement of the tongue body during the sequence [kai] offered reliable kinematic landmarks.

The local maxima in the tongue movement were associated with the constriction of [k] and the maximum closing at the offset of the diphthong [ai] and the local minimum was associated with the maximum vocal tract opening at the onset of the diphthong [ai].
text.formatted: The local maxima in the tongue movement were associated with the constriction of [k] and the maximum closing at the offset of the diphthong <ref type="bibr">[ai]</ref> and the local minimum was associated with the maximum vocal tract opening at the onset of the diphthong [ai].

text.text: However, for two talkers with ALS and one talker with HD, the tongue body movement of all ten sentence repetitions did not contain the second local maximum.
Another talker with HD could only produce the second local maximum in two of ten sentence repetitions.
When the second local maximum was missing, the diphthong was either severely distorted or replaced by the vowel [a] and a glottal stop.
In these cases, phase angles could not be calculated.

Using SMASH [34], the vertical tongue movement and the vertical jaw movement were trimmed using the local maxima the tongue body associated with [k] and the offset of the diphthong [ai] as the onset and offset of the tongue body cycle.

After spatial normalization of the tongue position and velocity signal, the normalized tongue body position and velocity value at the time of the jaw reaching the positional minimum (marked with red circles) was extracted to calculate the phase angle.
To compute phase angles, position and velocity signals were mapped onto a phase plane.

Because position (mm) and velocity (mm/s) rely on different physical units, both variables were normalized to the numerical interval [-1, +1] within each movement cycle prior to applying the inverse tangent function, following the classic procedure described by Kelso et al [6].

For each participant, ten repetitions were analyzed unless there were not ten repetitions available due to accidental speech errors (e.g., mispronouncing the target word), miscounting of trials, or missing positional landmarks.
In addition to the already mentioned missing second local maximum of the tongue body, there were four instances where the jaw did not produce a local minimum during the tongue body cycle.
In these cases, the jaw was continuously raised during the tongue body cycle.
These trials were also excluded.
Missing or excluded productions were evenly distributed across the cohort rather than clustered in a small number of participants.
In total, 1,066 out of 1,100 productions (96.9%) were submitted to the statistical analysis.
All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS Version 32.0.

To select the appropriate statistical tests to assess group effects on tongue body cycle durations, jaw opening amplitudes, and phase angles, data distributions were evaluated for normality, skewness and influential outliers using visual inspections (i.e., histograms and box plots).
We found that the distributions for the jaw opening amplitudes were positively skewed.
Therefore, we used a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with gamma distributions and log link to test for between-group differences in jaw opening amplitudes.
In the GLLM we used the residual method to determine the degrees of freedom and a robust estimation to handle violations of the model assumptions.
Phase angle distributions and tongue body cycle durations were not skewed but included some extreme values.
Extreme values were defined as values that were more than three times of the interquartile range away from the edge of the first or third quartile (e.g., [37, 38]).

This study investigated inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue body and jaw in talkers with different neurological conditions (i.e., PD, HD, MS, and ALS).
First, we tested for between-group differences in tongue body cycle durations and jaw opening amplitudes.

Findings for between-group differences in tongue body cycle duration aligned with previous reports of acoustic studies on speaking rate abnormalities in talkers with PD, ALS, MS and CON [e.g., [39] [40] [41].

text.text: That is, talkers with ALS and MS had significantly longer tongue body cycle durations indicating that their speaking rates were slower than those of talkers with PD and CON.

Findings of comparable tongue body cycle durations in talkers with HD and CON differed from previous reports of prolonged segment durations and slowed speaking rates in talkers with HD [37, 38]; however, they aligned with reports of a dysarthria subgroups of talkers with HD with an unaffected speaking rate [36].

text.text: That is, talkers with ALS had significantly larger jaw opening amplitudes than talkers with PD and CON and tended to be larger than those of talkers with MS and HD.

With regards to inter-articulatory timing patterns, we examined phase angles and expected them to be smaller or larger than 180 degrees in talkers with HD, MS, and PD due to less synchronized movements given that their neuropathologies involve impairment of the basal ganglia or cerebellar control circuits.
In addition, phase angles of talkers with ALS were expected to be close to 180 degrees given their potential overreliance on the jaw and limited independent tongue movements during speech.
However, our findings did not support this hypothesis.
We found that phase angles of talkers with ALS were significantly greater than those of talkers with MS, PD, HD, and typical talkers.
Although talkers with ALS produced abnormally large jaw movements, they did not exhibit more synchronized tongue and jaw movements than talkers with MS, PD, HD, or typical talkers.

Specifically, their phase angles were on average 8.4 degrees above 180 degrees while talkers with HD, MS, PD and typical talkers were on average between 5.3 degrees (talkers with HD) and 8.3 degrees (talkers with MS) below 180 degrees.
A weak positive correlation was observed between jaw opening amplitudes and phase angles when considering all talkers and when considering only typical talkers.

This finding suggests that the size of the jaw movement cannot be the main driver of the between-group differences in phase angles, especially because the weak positive association between jaw opening amplitudes and phase angles observed across all talkers was predominantly driven by the articulatory performance of typical talkers, not by talkers with ALS.
Alternatively, we examined if phase angles vary with speech rate abnormalities across these clinical groups given previous findings of speech rate effects on phase angles in typical talkers.
That is, talkers with MS and ALS, and potentially also talkers with HD, were expected to differ in their phase angles from talkers with PD and typical talkers due to their speech rate differences.
However, our findings did not support this hypothesis.
Only talkers with ALS but not talkers with MS differed in their phase angles from those of talkers with PD and typical talkers.
No significant association between cycle duration and phase angles were observed when considering all talkers or when considering only talkers within the same group.
Our findings highlight an important distinction between habitual speaking rate differences and experimentally elicited rate manipulations.

While previous studies demonstrated that cued changes in speaking rate (e.g., instructing a speaker to speak faster or slower) can systematically alter phase angles, our results indicate that habitual cycle durations do not exert the same driving effect.

Specifically, despite significant differences in habitual tongue body cycle durations across clinical and control groups, no significant associations between cycle duration and phase angles were observed.

This suggests that a speaker's intrinsic, habitual rate, whether typical or slowed due to pathology, does not inherently constrain inter-articulatory timing in the same manner as a targeted rate adjustment paradigm.
Talkers with ALS had significantly greater phase angles than talkers with HD, MS, PD, and typical talkers.
On average, phase angles of talkers with ALS were greater than 180 degrees, which indicates that the tongue body commonly reached the positional minimum at the diphthong onset before the jaw.
In fact, only five of the 17 talkers with ALS (29%) did not follow this pattern and had phase angles smaller than 180 degrees.
By contrast, the average phase angles of typical talkers, talkers with MS, PD, and HD were smaller than 180 degrees, which indicates that the jaw commonly reached the target before the tongue body.

More specifically, only ten of the 34 CON (29%), two of the 18 talkers with MS (11%), five of the 24 talkers with PD (21%), and six of the 17 talkers with HD (35%) did not follow this pattern and had phase angles that were greater than 180 degrees.
Thus, with regards to the order in which the articulators reached the target, the inter-articulatory timing patterns were fairly robust within each group.

It is important to point out that because the current study used the tongue body as the reference articulator and not the jaw, phase angles should be smaller at longer tongue body cycle durations to align with previous findings on cued slow speech effects [13].

text.text: That is because phase angles below 180 degrees indicate that the jaw leads the tongue when the tongue body is the reference (current study) whereas phase angles above 180 degree indicate that the jaw leads the tongue when the jaw is the reference sensor (previous studies).
Therefore, the observed phase angles of most talkers with ALS in the current study do not align with the inter-articulatory timing pattern previously observed for cued slow speech in typical talkers.

The discrepancies between the findings for phase angles under cued slow speech in typical talkers and those for phase angles of talkers with ALS who spoke at their habitual albeit abnormally slow rate suggest that the absolute movement duration, or the absolute speech rate, may not determine a talker's inter-articulatory timing pattern.
This notion is supposed by our correlational analysis of tongue body cycle durations and phase angles, which did not yield a significant finding.
Thus, it may rather be the speech task (i.e., the execution of a cued slow speech rate) that determines the inter-articulatory timing pattern.
Indeed, previous studies revealed speech rate effects on phase angles in typical talkers [8, 13, 15].

text.text: However, in these studies, talkers were cued to increase or reduce their speaking rate.
In the current study, talkers were asked to speak at their habitual rate, which resulted a wide range of tongue body cycle durations across talkers due to their dysarthria.
Especially talkers with MS and ALS had significantly longer tongue body cycle durations than CON, talkers with PD, and talkers with HD.
However, the absolute tongue body cycle duration, which indirectly characterized a talker's speech rate, was not predictive of their inter-articulatory timing pattern.

To better understand the unique interarticulatory timing pattern of talkers with ALS, future studies could examine if speaking rate modifications elicit changes in the phase angles of talkers with ALS.

Such insights would help determine if talkers with ALS are constrained to their specific inter-articulatory timing pattern due to their disease or if they are able to modify their inter-articulatory timing patterns in response to various speech task demands.
No significant differences in phase angles were found between typical talkers, talkers with MS, HD, and PD.

The lack of significant differences in inter-articulatory timing patterns between typical talkers and talkers with PD and MS contradicts findings of disrupted timing patterns of limb motor control studies [43] [44] [45], whereas the lack of group-level differences in HD may be attributable to high individual variability which will be discussed later on.

Although not evident in the group level plots, we would like to point out differences in inter-articulatory timing patterns at the individual performance level.
Specifically, we noted that phase angles varied greatly across repetitions within each talker with HD.

For example, the phase angle's coefficient of variation across trials was on average 11.4 degrees for talkers with HD whereas the coefficient of variation for talkers with PD, MS, ALS and typical talkers was on average much lower (3.9 degrees in ALS, 6.4 degrees in MS, 5.8 degrees in PD, and 7.5 degrees in CON).

This observation suggests that although phase angles of talkers with HD did not significantly differ from the other clinical groups and typical talkers, the basal ganglia pathology may negatively impact the ability to produce a consistent inter-articulatory timing pattern in talkers with HD.
In the current study, we chose to characterize inter-articulatory timing patterns by measuring phase angles.

Phase angles are expressed relative to 360 degrees regardless of the duration of the cycle and are heavily influenced by the shape of the movement trajectory towards and away from the target position (i.e., maximum opening position).
However, it should be noted that phase angles do not provide the same insights as the latency measure (i.e., temporal lag).

Although a greater latency is typically associated with a phase angle that is much smaller or larger than 180 degrees, a specific phase angle can have slightly different latencies and a specific latency can have slightly different phase angles.
That is because the shape of the movement trajectory of the articulator that serves as the reference signal impacts the phase angle more than the latency itself.

For example, if the shape of the tongue movement trajectory is characterized by a plateau around the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai], phase angles will be closer to 180 degrees even if there is a relatively small lag between the jaw and tongue.

By contrast, if the movement trajectory of the tongue is characterized by more "peakedness" towards and away from the maximum opening position, relatively small lags between the tongue and jaw can produce phase angles that are disproportionally smaller or larger than 180 degrees.

Due to these concerns, we informally tested the strength of association between latencies and phase angles by extracting the lag durations between the tongue and the jaw reaching the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai] together with the phase angles across all repetitions of all talkers.

text.text: Thus, the reported phase angles in the current study can provide good insights in the extent to which tongue and jaw movements are synchronized.
Previous studies investigated inter-articulatory timing patterns by expressing the timing of the articulator of interest (tongue, upper lip, lower lip) with respect to the jaw cycle .

In the current study, the tongue cycle was taken as reference to which the timing of the jaw reaching the maximal opening of the jaw at the onset of the diphthong /ai/ was expressed, which limits the comparability to previous studies.

However, with cycle durations of typical talkers in the current study being comparable to those of a slow speech condition in previous studies, the phase angles of our typical talkers were well-aligned with those of previous studies when accounting for the different reference articulator [8, 13].

text.text: That is, the average phase angle for our control group was about 172 degrees indicating that the jaw led the tongue body.
The average phase angle of ten talkers in Masapolo and Nittrouer's study [8] was about 200 degrees, also indicating that the jaw led the tongue tip in typical talkers.
text.formatted: The average phase angle of ten talkers in Masapolo and Nittrouer's study <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> was about 200 degrees, also indicating that the jaw led the tongue tip in typical talkers.

text.text: Mathematically, phase relations measure relative spatiotemporal coupling regardless of which articulator is assigned as the reference frame.
Therefore, we believe that our approach of using the tongue body as the reference was well-suited to study interarticulatory timing patterns, specifically to explore the jaw-tongue coupling patterns.

However, future studies should investigate inter-articulatory timing patterns with the traditional approach of using the jaw as the reference signal to replicate and further extend current study findings on talkers with dysarthria.

Furthermore, a major difference in the experimental design between the current and previous studies was that the target utterance did not contain two stop consonants, such as [tad, bab, bak, tak], but [kai].
text.formatted: Furthermore, a major difference in the experimental design between the current and previous studies was that the target utterance did not contain two stop consonants, such as [tad, bab, bak, tak], but <ref type="bibr">[kai]</ref>.

text.text: However, the offset of the diphthong [ai] at the end of the tongue body cycle also required a vocal tract constriction that was consistently executed by the tongue body.
Although, the jaw was consistently lowered to produce the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai], it was not consistently raised during the diphthong.
However, the jaw was always elevated after reaching the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai] and eventually supported the constriction of [k] in "kite".

Nevertheless, due to the presence of reliable landmarks for the tongue body and jaw to reach the maximum opening position and initiate the upward movement towards vocal tract constriction at the offset of the diphthong [ai], we argue that the sequence [kai] was also well-suited to study inter-articulatory timing patterns.
Another major difference between the current study and previous studies is that we could not decouple the jaw from the tongue.

Decoupling jaw movements from the posterior tongue is challenging because the jaw movements are recorded more anteriorly in the vocal tract where, due to jaw rotation, the movement amplitudes of the jaw are larger than at the location of the posterior tongue.

A linear subtraction of jaw movement from the posterior tongue, which is an approach commonly used to decouple the lower lip or the tongue tip from the jaw, would not yield accurate data of independent posterior tongue movement [36].
text.formatted: A linear subtraction of jaw movement from the posterior tongue, which is an approach commonly used to decouple the lower lip or the tongue tip from the jaw, would not yield accurate data of independent posterior tongue movement <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, the timing of the tongue and jaw reaching the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai] was asynchronous in most cases (983 out of 1066 productions, 92%) indicating that independent tongue movements are reflected in the tongue movement trajectory.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the timing of the tongue and jaw reaching the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong <ref type="bibr">[ai]</ref> was asynchronous in most cases (983 out of 1066 productions, 92%) indicating that independent tongue movements are reflected in the tongue movement trajectory.

text.text: However, the shape of the tongue movement could be partially affected by the jaw in the current study and this could impact the specific value of the phase angle.

However, it would not affect whether a phase angle was smaller or larger than 180 degrees because the order of the articulators reaching the target and not the specific tongue position and velocity determines whether a phase angle is smaller or larger than 180 degrees (i.e., if the jaw is reaching the target before the tongue, the phase angle is smaller than 180 degrees if the tongue body is the reference signal).

Therefore, the overall finding of the current study, which suggest that talkers with ALS differ in their inter-articulatory timing patterns from talkers with PD, MS, HD, and typical talkers was primarily driven by the order of the articulators reaching the maximum opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai].

text.text: Nevertheless, it is important to develop a decoupling algorithm that can accurately determine independent posterior tongue movements for future studies to replicate the current findings.
In the current study, we did not control for medication status in talkers with HD and surgical intervention (DBS) in talkers with PD.
However, we did not observe any systematic differences in phase angles due to the medication status in talkers with HD.

One talker with HD on medication produced the largest phase angles of the HD group while two other talkers with HD on medication had very small phase angles and the remaining three talkers with HD on medication fell somewhere in the middle of the group's distribution.
Similarly, two of the three talkers with PD who had undergone DBS treatment had phase angles comparable to those of talkers with PD who did not have DBS.
The third talker with DBS produced the largest phase angles of all talkers with PD.
Thus, no systematic pattern could be detected that suggest medication status or DBS could be considered confounding factors.
Finally, future studies are needed to examine inter-articulatory timing patterns across a wide range of phonetic contexts to determine if current findings generalize or if they are stimulus-specific.

Future studies should also include the tongue tip and jaw as well as the upper lip and lower lip or jaw as articulators of interest to determine if inter-articulatory timing patterns reveal similar disease-related group differences.
This study investigated temporal, spatial and spatiotemporal alterations between tongue body and jaw movements across several diseases.
While tongue body cycle durations were significantly prolonged in ALS and MS, jaw amplitudes were enlarged specifically in ALS.
Inter-articulatory phase angles differentiated ALS from all other cohorts.
Talkers with ALS exhibited significantly larger phase angles compared to PD, HD, and MS groups, whose phase angles remained comparable to typical talkers.
This highlights distinct spatiotemporal timing profiles in ALS that evolve largely independently of speech rate or jaw amplitude variations.

text.text: Tongue 454 body cycle duration was measured based on the tongue kinematic signal as the time interval between onset and offset of tongue body movement during the target sequence[kai].

Jaw amplitudes were measured as the relative positional change of the jaw from the positional maximum associated with [k] to the positional minimum associated with the onset of the diphthong [ai] during the tongue body cycle.

To quantify the inter-articulatory timing pattern of the tongue body and the jaw, the phase angle (φ) was calculated based on the timing of the maximum opening of the jaw relative to the tongue cycle.
The local minimum of the jaw was identified algorithmically within the Matlab script.

Using the spatially normalized tongue body signal and its first derivative (velocity), the tongue body velocity and the tongue body position at the time of the local minimum of the jaw were extracted.
In a few instances the jaw produced multiple local minima.
In these cases, the lowest of the local minima was selected to calculate the phase angle.
The phase angle of the tongue body was then calculated using Equation1.

Phase angle (φ) = arctan Because the tongue body cycle is used as the reference in the current study, phase angles smaller than 180° indicate that the jaw reached the maximum opening position earlier and initiated the upward movement towards vocal tract constriction sooner than the tongue body.
Phase angles larger than 180° indicate that the jaw reached the maximum opening position after the tongue body and initiated upward movement towards vocal tract constriction later.
Values of 180° indicate that the jaw and tongue reached their maximum opening positions at the same time and initiated the upward movement towards vocal tract constriction simultaneously.
